>    184	## 5. Marca alheia — a regra estreita
>    185	
>    186	**Uso nominativo** (New Kids, 9º Circ. 1992) exige **cumulativamente**: (1) não dá para identificar
>    187	sem a marca; (2) **só o necessário**; (3) nada sugere endosso. Vídeo editorial comparando modelos
>    188	satisfaz (1) trivialmente.
>    189	
>    190	**Mas o logo é o que consome o fator 2** (Toyota v. Tabari, 2010): a corte notou que os réus podiam
>    191	comunicar *"without using the **visual trappings** of the Lexus brand"* — usaram a palavra, não o logo.
>    192	Por isso o único `role` que assino é `rotulo-de-dado`.
>    193	
>    194	**As 5 proibições comuns a todas as guidelines legíveis:** não recolorir · não distorcer/esticar/girar ·
>    195	não sugerir parceria · não incorporar no seu lockup · não dar proeminência maior que a sua.
>    196	Anthropic é a mais dura no texto (*"No alterations … color, font, proportion, or otherwise"*, sem
>    197	ressalva referencial); Google permite referência *"**in plain text**"* — o **nome**, não o logo.
>    198	
>    199	**O logo animado pode:** entrar/sair (opacidade, posição), ganhar/perder placa, ser revelado por
>    200	máscara **externa**. **Nunca:** deformar, girar, mudar de cor, piscar em cor alheia.
>    201	
>    202	**Nuance:** guideline é declaração unilateral — vincula licenciados, **não extingue** o uso nominativo
>    203	de terceiro. Mas é **evidência** do que o titular considera confusório. **Nada aqui é aconselhamento
>    204	jurídico**, e o canal é monetizado promovendo produto da casa — o que enfraquece o enquadramento
>    205	puramente editorial. Primeira peça com logo real merece revisão de advogado (decisão do Owner).
>    206

## 🤖 Claude *(17:04:32)*

<details>
<summary>💭 Thinking Process</summary>

I found the issue — the `.icon-disc` element applies a 3D rotation and scale based on time and interaction, while the `#hero` container has its own separate 3D transforms. The problem is that `getBoundingClientRect().width` captures the foreshortened dimensions after both the parent's perspective rotation and scaling are applied, so the measurement method needs to account for this compounding effect.

The G7 gate checking "spread ≤ 10%" becomes unreliable because the hero's scale oscillates ±1.5% continuously due to the sine wave in its transform, which means any width measurement varies by up to 3% peak-to-peak depending on when you sample it. The seed lottery creating a 31% spread (54 vs 71 pixels) is real and measurable, but the gate itself can't reliably enforce a fixed threshold when the underlying dimensions are time-dependent.

More critically, the pixel calculation `round(min(W,H)*(0.135+0.02*((seed>>>(ic*2))%3)))` produces only three possible values (0.135, 0.155, 0.175), which gives a minimum 23% spread across the icon set — so the Art Director can't actually satisfy a ≤10% constraint at all since it's entirely governed by the seed derived from the title and description. The stroke calculations are checking out — the fixed stroke-widths scale proportionally with the rendered sizes, and the hero SVG dimensions are within expected tolerances of the computed values, so the math is internally consistent.

Now I need to verify the beatIndex transport claim, which is the key discovery and central to understanding G10.

</details>

Let me verify the G5 claim about min/max ratios: the skill specifies that G5 passes if min/max < 0.8, or if delta or a tie is declared. The probe's own data shows 64.5/76.8 = 0.8398, which exceeds 0.8 and fails the first condition, so it needs to satisfy the delta or tie clause instead.

For G7, the 10% optical spread gate is structurally tied to the seed and contaminated by the rotateY+scale animation. Looking at the pixel bucket ratios—0.135/0.155 gives 13% spread, 0.135/0.175 gives 23%, and 0.155/0.175 gives 11%—any two icons in different buckets exceed the 10% threshold, so only identical buckets would pass.

With three icons, the probability all land in the same bucket is roughly 1/9, meaning G7 fails about 89% of the time. Since the pixel values derive from the seed (which comes from the title and description), the Art Director can't fix this—it's locked in by Dramaturgo's text. The skill acknowledges this through VOC-ART-002, but listing G7 as a per-scene gate effectively means blocking ~89% of scenes that use contextIcons, which is a severe constraint that isn't explicitly stated as such.

The measurement method also uses getBoundingClientRect with dynamic transforms—scale varies from 0.85 to 1.0 depending on the animation state, and the hero element oscillates with a sine wave that adds up to ±1.5% variation. The rotateY transform introduces foreshortening that shifts measurements by up to 1.23%, so the same scene measured at different times produces different results.

This ±1.2% to ±1.9% jitter is small relative to the 10% threshold, but it matters at the boundary where buckets cluster around 11%, 13%, and 23%—making the measurement unreliable at the margin. The real fix is to read the pixel values directly from the DOM style attribute instead of relying on getBoundingClientRect, which would eliminate the time-dependent variation.

## 🤖 Claude *(17:11:31)*

<details>
<summary>💭 Thinking Process</summary>

The KPI benchmark shows the real constraint: the performance target for the Art Director's layer is under 400 ms/frame, but that's actually the ceiling for the entire scene—not just the additive work. So framing it as "what I draw must cost less than 400 ms/frame" creates an almost impossible requirement since the budget needs to account for everything else already rendering.

Looking at the glyph list, I can see the four SVG paths map to bot, server, money, and bot again—so three distinct icons plus the hero. The six brands all resolve to the `bot` keyword in the icon library, which includes entries like "gpt", "claude", "qwen", "gemini", "grok", and "llm", so the mapping is consistent even though DeepSeek isn't explicitly listed.

Now examining the optical weight spread KPI: it claims 30% as the current state with a ≤10% target, but the actual ratio of hero to disc stroke is 2.19 (219%), not 30%—that 30% is only measuring the disc-to-disc variation. The KPI conflates two different measurements in one cell, and the ≤10% target creates a real tension: if it applies to the hero-to-disc ratio, hitting that target would require nearly identical stroke weights, which would flatten the visual hierarchy the hero is supposed to establish. This looks like a measurement ambiguity that needs clarification.

On achievability: the pixel bucket system produces 13%/11%/23% spreads across different sizes, so hitting ≤10% for discs alone is mathematically impossible about 89% of the time when multiple icons land in different buckets. Since the Art Director can't change the pixel buckets, this KPI becomes unactionable as written—and it's marked as a hard gate, meaning the team would have to reject most contextIcon scenarios. The fallback (removing contextIcons entirely) sidesteps the problem, but that consequence isn't surfaced in the gate definition.

There's also a measurement contamination issue: getBoundingClientRect picks up the rotateY transform (±1.23%) and the hero's scale oscillation (±1.5%), so the same scene produces different G7 readings depending on when you measure it. At a 10% threshold with 11% real spread, this timing jitter can flip the pass/fail verdict. The gate should measure the authored pixel width directly instead of the rendered bounding box to avoid this noise.

I've now confirmed the measured values match the transform math exactly — the 62.6/63 and 70.1/71 ratios correspond to specific rotateY angles (around 6.4° and 9.1°) at different time phases, which checks out perfectly against the animation formula.

The hero element shows similar contamination: the authored 137 value gets scaled down to about 135.1 through a combination of rotateY and scale transforms, which I can verify through the same trigonometric breakdown.

The scale itself oscillates by ±1.5% over time, which means the KPI ratio of 2.19× isn't actually fixed—it drifts between roughly 2.16 and 2.22 depending on the animation phase. That's fine for visual magnitude but problematic if this number's being used as a hard threshold.

Now I need to verify whether the proposal's fallback approach in section 11.3 actually works end-to-end with the badge/seal requirement.

</details>
